items.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Years later, I heard this song by Horace Silver... I said, oh, that’s where I got my melody to Blues in Hoss Flat.

ctx.x: How often in your work as a arranger or composer, I guess more as a composer, are you utilizing things like you thought you heard with Shiny Stockings, that is, you’re elaborating, embellishing, renewing, tinkering with, however you want to say it, with various variations here, some kernel of an idea that you heard somebody fiddle with?

I suspect more often than I might even realize, because things that I put forth as my originals contain phrases that I imagine that I came up with myself, but they must have come from somewhere. When I first wrote Blues in Hoss Flat, that opening statement by the trombones [Foster sings these four bars] and the trumpets [Foster sings the trumpet punctuations and then the trombone phrase again]. That sounded to me like a fairly trite phrase [Foster sings the trombone phrase again], but I said, in spite of its…
How typical do you think that is in music?
